# The Honesty of Dishonesty

## When Being Good Stops Working

Law 12's whole method is a single honest or generous act deployed to lower someone's guard. Its Reversal names the condition under which that becomes impossible:

> *When you have a history of deceit behind you, no amount of honesty, generosity, or kindness will fool people. In fact it will only call attention to itself. Once people have come to see you as deceitful, to act honest all of a sudden is simply suspicious. In these cases it is better to play the rogue.*[^1]

*It will only call attention to itself.*

That is the mechanism, and it is precise. The gesture does not merely fail to persuade — it becomes **evidence**. A known deceiver behaving generously has done something out of character, and out-of-character behaviour is exactly what a wary observer is scanning for.

So the reputation you have already built determines which moves are available, and this is the rare place where Greene acknowledges that a technique can be foreclosed by your own history.

## The Eiffel Tower, and the Man Who Went Cold

Lustig is about to sell the Eiffel Tower to an industrialist who believes the government is auctioning it for scrap. He has successfully impersonated a government official. The money is about to change hands.

And at the last minute the mark hesitates. *"Something about Lustig bothered him."*[^2]

Lustig senses it. What he does next is the page:

> *Leaning over to the industrialist, Lustig explained, in a low whisper, how low his salary was, how difficult his finances were, on and on. After a few minutes of this, the industrialist realized that Lustig was asking for a bribe. For the first time he relaxed.*[^2]

The mark relaxes **because he is being asked for a bribe.**

Greene's explanation: *"Now he knew he could trust Lustig: Since all government officials were dishonest, Lustig had to be real."*[^2]

## Analytical Case Study: The Mark Had a Model, and Lustig Fed It

This is the transferable content and it is worth taking apart carefully, because the move is counterintuitive in a specific way.

The industrialist's suspicion was not *this man may be a criminal.* It was something vaguer — *something about this doesn't fit.*

What did not fit was that the official was too clean. A real French government official, in this man's model of the world, would be on the take. Lustig had been performing an honesty that the mark's own experience said did not exist in that role.

So Lustig supplies **the missing corruption**, and the discrepancy resolves.

The critical feature: the mark's model of the world was **accurate**, or at least sincerely held, and it was doing exactly the work suspicion is supposed to do. He detected a genuine anomaly. What he could not do was interpret it correctly, because the anomaly had two explanations — *this man is not a real official* and *this official is unusually honest* — and Lustig offered him a third that was cheaper than either.

**Confirming someone's cynicism is a way of confirming that you are real**, and cynical people are disproportionately vulnerable to it, because their model has fewer honest people in it and therefore fewer ways to explain a clean actor.

## Talleyrand's Version, Which Is Larger

The second case runs the same principle as a lifetime policy rather than a save:

> *As the French diplomat Talleyrand grew older, his reputation as a master liar and deceiver spread. At the Congress of Vienna (1814-1815), he would spin fabulous stories and make impossible remarks to people who knew he had to be lying. His dishonesty had no purpose except to cloak the moments when he really was deceiving them.*[^3]

*His dishonesty had no purpose except to cloak the moments when he really was deceiving them.*

That is a **noise strategy**, and it is structurally different from Lustig's. Lustig fixed one discrepancy in one meeting. Talleyrand generated continuous, obvious, purposeless falsehood so that the signal-to-noise ratio around him collapsed.

## "In Business One Ought to Show One's Hand"

The worked example is the sharpest thing in the passage: among friends, Talleyrand said *"with apparent sincerity"* — *"In business one ought to show one's hand."*[^3]

> *No one who heard him could believe their ears: A man who never once in his life had shown his cards was telling other people to show theirs.*[^3]

The statement is not a lie anyone could act on. It is **transparently false**, said sincerely, to people who know it is false. Its only function is to be an instance of Talleyrand lying for no reason.

And the effect, in Greene's words: *"Tactics like this made it impossible to distinguish Talleyrand's real deceptions from his fake ones. By embracing his reputation for dishonesty, he preserved his ability to deceive."*[^3]

## The Two Are Not the Same Technique

Worth separating, because the chapter runs them together and they have different requirements.

**Lustig's move is corrective.** One discrepancy, detected in real time, patched by supplying the expected flaw. It requires reading the mark's model accurately and fast, and it works once, in a specific transaction.

**Talleyrand's is structural.** A standing policy of visible, costless dishonesty maintained over years, which degrades everyone's ability to detect the expensive kind. It requires no read of any individual and it protects every future operation.

The second is far more powerful and requires something the first does not: **a position secure enough to survive being known as a liar.** Talleyrand could afford a public reputation for deceit because he was indispensable at the Congress of Vienna. Almost nobody else can.

Which is the same shape logged repeatedly in this build — the most effective version of a technique turns out to require standing the ordinary reader does not have.

## Embracing the Reputation

Greene's general statement is the law's real contribution:

> *Nothing in the realm of power is set in stone. Overt deceptiveness will sometimes cover your tracks, even making you admired for the honesty of your dishonesty.*[^4]

*Admired for the honesty of your dishonesty.*

The phrase is doing something clever. A person who is openly, consistently, unapologetically a rogue is legible — and legibility reads as a kind of integrity. You know where you stand with them. The disguise is dropped, so there is apparently nothing left to look for.

That perceived transparency is the cover. Which means the Reversal is not the opposite of Law 12 at all: **both work by supplying the observer with a stable classification of you, and then operating inside it.** Selective honesty installs *this person is honest.* The rogue strategy installs *this person is a known rogue, so I am on my guard and therefore safe.*

Either way the target stops actively investigating, which is the only thing the operator needs.

## Implementation Workflow

Your reputation has hardened and a sincere gesture would now read as a manoeuvre.

**First, check what your reputation actually forecloses.** Greene's opening claim is the useful one: if people have classified you as deceitful, a sudden honest act is not neutral — it is an anomaly that draws attention. Know which moves your history has taken off the table.

**Second, find the discrepancy the other party has actually noticed.** Lustig did not defend himself in general. He identified the one thing that did not fit the mark's model of a government official and supplied it.

**Third, consider that the missing piece may be a flaw.** This is the counterintuitive core. When someone is uneasy about you, the resolution is sometimes a *worse* fact about you, not a better one, because it restores coherence.

**Fourth, if you must be known as a rogue, be legibly one.** Consistency is what converts a bad reputation into a stable classification, and stable classifications stop being investigated.

**Fifth, notice what this costs.** Talleyrand's strategy required a position secure enough to be openly known as a liar. Adopting it without that position simply means being known as a liar.

And the plain record: this is advice on how to keep deceiving people once you are known for deceiving people, and the second case is a diplomat who manufactured pointless falsehoods for years specifically so that his real ones would not be findable.

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

**Strongest support.** Two cases with clearly different architectures — one corrective, one structural — and a stated mechanism for each. The Talleyrand *"show one's hand"* example is unusually well chosen, because its transparent falsity is the entire point rather than an incidental detail.

**Tension — the Reversal is not a reversal.** Both the law and its Reversal work by installing a stable classification and operating inside it. Greene presents them as opposites; they are the same mechanism with different labels.

**Tension — the two cases are conflated.** A real-time save requiring an accurate read of one person, and a multi-year noise policy requiring exceptional standing, are presented as one technique.

**Tension — it needs the mark's cynicism to be *correct*.** Lustig's move works because French officials plausibly did take bribes. Against someone whose model of the world contains honest officials, supplying corruption confirms the wrong thing. The technique is parasitic on an accurate cynicism it did not create.

🚩 SINGLE SOURCE · 🚩 SECONDARY WITHOUT PRIMARY — no citation for either case. The Eiffel Tower con is historically attested in outline; **the whispered-bribe detail and the mark's internal reasoning are given without support**, and Talleyrand's remark among friends is reported with no source, date or company named. `[POPULAR SOURCE]`

**Open questions.**

- If both the law and its Reversal work by installing a classification, is the real principle simply *be legible*, with honesty and roguery as two available legibilities?
- Talleyrand's noise strategy requires being indispensable enough to survive the reputation. Is there a version available to someone without standing, or does that leave only Lustig's one-shot save?

## Author Tensions & Convergences

This Reversal sits directly against [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/giving-before-you-take|Giving Before You Take]], and the pair reveals what Law 12 is really about.

The law's mechanism: a first-encounter act of honesty installs a favourable prior, and subsequent evidence gets filed under it. Gould saw *"many clues"* and misread every one.

The Reversal's mechanism: an established reputation for deceit installs a *different* prior — and Talleyrand's insight is that this prior is **also exploitable**, because a target who has classified you as a known liar believes they have already accounted for you.

**So the operative asset in both directions is the same: a settled classification in the other person's head.** What varies is only its content.

That explains why Greene's advice on both sides is *consistency* — a series of inconsequential honest acts in the law, a series of pointless lies in the Reversal. The content is arbitrary; the **stability** is the product.

And it produces the finding the chapter does not state: **the dangerous person is not the one you have classified wrongly, it is the one you have classified at all.** Both of Law 12's mechanisms exploit the fact that a resolved question stops being asked, and neither requires the classification to be false.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

**→ business · [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/gould-and-lord-gordon-gordon|Gould and Lord Gordon-Gordon]]**

Gordon-Gordon proves the Erie forgeries came from inside the company, wins Gould's gratitude, trades on it for years, then dumps his stock and vanishes — and Greene notes that *"there had been many clues"* which Gould's initial classification prevented him from reading.

Set against Lustig's whispered bribe, the two mark the same failure from opposite directions.

Gould had classified Gordon-Gordon as **trustworthy**, and every subsequent anomaly was filed as an exception.
The industrialist had *not yet* classified Lustig, was actively uneasy, and Lustig's move was to **supply the classification himself** before the mark reached one of his own.

The insight neither page produces alone: the vulnerable moment is not when you are trusting, it is when you are **resolving.** Gould's damage was done at the first meeting; the industrialist's at the whisper. In both, the operator supplied the frame during the short window in which the target was actively deciding what kind of person they were dealing with.

Which gives a defensive rule that fits both: **be most careful about the evidence that arrives while you are still forming a view**, because that evidence sets the interpreter for everything after it — and an operator who understands this will concentrate their entire effort there.

**→ history · [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/the-bland-exterior|The Bland Exterior]]**

At Law 3, Talleyrand's standing technique: *"never was a face less of a barometer"* — a surface that gives nothing away, alongside Kissinger boring negotiators into submission before hitting them with terms.

The same man appears here running the opposite policy: spinning *"fabulous stories and impossible remarks"* to people who knew he was lying.

Those look contradictory and are not, and the pair resolves it.

The bland exterior manages the **channel** — nothing legible leaves. The fabulous stories manage the **archive** — the record of Talleyrand's statements is so thoroughly contaminated that no individual statement can be weighed.

The insight the pair produces: a person maintaining a deception over decades has two separate problems, and they need opposite instruments. Moment-to-moment leakage is solved by giving nothing; long-run pattern analysis is solved by giving far too much of no value. **Silence protects the instant and noise protects the history**, and Greene builds each into a different law without noticing they are one operator's complete system.

That also explains why Talleyrand survives four regimes while more brilliant men do not. He is not better at any single deception; he has solved the **auditing** problem, which is the one that actually catches people.

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication.** The industrialist's suspicion was working correctly — he had detected a genuine anomaly, that the official was implausibly clean — and Lustig defeated it by supplying **a worse fact about himself.** The resolution to *something doesn't fit* was corruption, not virtue. **Confirming someone's cynicism is a way of proving you are real**, which makes accurately cynical people specifically vulnerable, since their model contains fewer honest actors and therefore fewer ways to explain a clean one.

**Generative questions.**

- If both the law and its Reversal install a stable classification and operate inside it, is the real vulnerability *having resolved the question* rather than having resolved it wrongly?
- Talleyrand's noise strategy contaminates his own archive. Is that available to anyone whose statements are recorded and searchable — or has it been foreclosed by the record-keeping of the last century?
- Lustig's move needs the mark's cynicism to be accurate. **What is the equivalent when a target's model of the world is wrong** — do you supply their imagined flaw instead?

# Three Death-Ground Tactics

## The Difference Between Having It Done to You and Doing It Yourself

Cortés had his men's ships scuttled without telling them. A czar staged Dostoyevsky's execution as psychological theater. Both stories are famous, both produced dramatic results, and neither is something you can actually apply to your own life without either coercing someone or waiting for a catastrophe.

These three tactics are the usable version. Same mechanism — remove an exit, produce urgency — but self-applied, consented to, and available on an ordinary Tuesday.[^1]

## Stake Everything on a Single Throw

In 1937, Lyndon Johnson was twenty-eight, working as the Texas director of the National Youth Administration, when Congressman James Buchanan suddenly died.[^1]

Texas voters returned incumbents reliably, which meant a congressional seat opened perhaps every ten or twenty years. Johnson wanted to be in Congress by thirty. He didn't have a decade to wait.

He also had no realistic path. He was young, effectively unknown in Buchanan's district, and would be running against political heavyweights the voters already favored. Losing badly wouldn't just waste money — the humiliation could derail his longer-term ambitions entirely.[^1]

He ran anyway. Over the following weeks he visited every backwater village in the district, shook the hand of every poor farmer he could find, sat in drugstores talking to people who had never spoken to a candidate before. Old-style rallies and barbecues, new-style radio ads, everything at once. By the time it was over he was hospitalized for exhaustion and appendicitis — and he'd won one of the great upsets in American political history.[^1]

### What the Tactic Actually Does

Greene's read is precise about the mechanism. Most people, facing uncertainty, hedge — attempting several things at once on the theory that one will pay off. The predictable result is diffused attention and half-hearted effort across all of them.[^1]

Staking everything on one throw isn't about courage. It's about removing the option to be half-hearted, which is the only thing that reliably produces the intensity Johnson brought to that campaign.

## Act Before You Are Ready

In 49 B.C., Roman senators allied with Pompey ordered Julius Caesar to disband his army or be declared a traitor. Caesar was in southern Gaul with only five thousand men — the bulk of his legions were far north, weeks away.[^1]

Obeying meant suicide. Waiting meant weeks of exposure while the Senate consolidated against him. Caesar chose a third option: "Let the die be cast," and crossed the Rubicon into Italy with the five thousand he had.

Leading troops onto Italian soil meant war with Rome. There was no reversing it. And because he'd committed with a fraction of his forces, he was compelled to concentrate everything, waste no one, move at speed, and improvise constantly.[^1] By seizing the initiative he frightened the Senate badly enough that Pompey fled the city.

### The Reasoning Underneath

Greene's argument here runs against ordinary prudence deliberately: we often wait too long specifically because no external pressure forces the decision, and readiness turns out to be a feeling that never quite arrives on its own.[^1]

Acting before you're ready produces two effects simultaneously. It surprises opponents who assumed you'd wait for full preparation. And it forces maximum use of whatever resources you actually have, because there's no longer a larger force coming to save the plan.

## Enter New Waters

MGM had made Joan Crawford — discovered her, built her stardom, crafted her public image. By the early 1940s, it was also casting her in the same undemanding roles repeatedly, and she had had enough.[^1]

In 1943, she did what almost no established star did voluntarily: she asked out of her contract, giving up guaranteed work, guaranteed income, and the institutional machinery that had built her career, in exchange for uncertainty.

### Why This One Is the Hardest

The Johnson and Caesar tactics both involve pressure you can feel building — a deadline, an ultimatum, an obvious crisis demanding a response. Crawford's situation had none of that. Nothing was going wrong. The work was steady, the money was good, and the only problem was that it had stopped being difficult.

That makes this the tactic most people never run, because comfort produces no signal that anything needs changing. Greene's point is that the absence of challenge is itself the danger — an environment that stops testing you produces a slow, unnoticed decline in capacity, and only leaving it makes that visible.

## Implementation Workflow

You've been comfortable in a role for about three years. The work is fine. You're good at it. Nothing is wrong, exactly, and that's the whole problem — you can feel yourself having stopped growing without being able to point to any specific thing that's failing.

Run the diagnostic across all three tactics rather than reaching for whichever is most familiar.

If your problem is that you're spreading effort across four half-committed projects, Johnson's tactic applies: pick one, drop the others visibly enough that returning to them would be embarrassing, and notice what happens to your working intensity within a week.

If your problem is that you keep waiting for conditions to be right before starting something you already know you want, Caesar's applies: commit publicly, with a date, before you feel prepared — and let the commitment force the preparation rather than the other way around.

If your problem is Crawford's — nothing wrong, nothing growing — then neither of the first two will help, because both assume a pressure that doesn't exist in your situation. The only move available is the hardest one: leave the comfortable thing before it fails, on no evidence except your own sense that it's stopped being difficult.

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

All three cases are well-documented historically. Johnson's 1937 upset, Caesar's Rubicon crossing, and Crawford's MGM departure are corroborated well beyond Greene's retelling. `[POPULAR SOURCE]` for Greene's framing and selection.

**Open tension**: all three are survivor cases, and the selection bias is severe in a specific way. Johnson won; had he lost badly, this would be a cautionary tale about a young man who destroyed his prospects through overreach. Caesar won; had he lost, the Rubicon crossing would read as a reckless gamble by a general who miscalculated his support. Crawford's post-MGM career succeeded; plenty of stars who left studio contracts simply disappeared.

The tactics describe what these three people did. They don't describe what distinguishes the people for whom it works from the people for whom the identical move is career-ending, and the chapter never raises that question.

**A second tension**: Johnson ended his campaign hospitalized. Greene mentions this as evidence of intensity rather than as a cost worth weighing. Total commitment has a physical price, and the chapter consistently frames that price as proof the technique is working.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Set this beside [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/cortes-and-the-burnt-ships|Cortés and the Burnt Ships]], the chapter's most famous case. Cortés's version is admired precisely because it was drastic and irreversible — but it was also imposed on five hundred people who never agreed to it. These three tactics are the same mechanism with consent restored: Johnson chose his own campaign, Caesar chose his own crossing, Crawford chose her own departure. Read together, they demonstrate that the coercive element in the Cortés story wasn't actually load-bearing for the psychology. Removing your own exit produces the same intensity as having it removed for you — which means the chapter's most-cited case is also its least necessary one.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

**Business → The Public Commitment as a Forcing Function.** Founders and operators routinely use announced launch dates, pre-sold products, and publicly stated targets as devices to make retreat socially expensive — the modern, low-stakes descendant of Caesar's Rubicon. The insight the pairing produces: what makes these work isn't the deadline itself but the *witnesses*. A private deadline can be quietly moved; a public one can't be moved without a cost that's felt immediately. The mechanism is reputational, not temporal, which is why "tell someone" is consistently better advice than "set a date."

**Psychology → Opportunity Cost and Cognitive Diffusion.** Research on decision-making under abundant options shows that having more alternatives available reliably reduces commitment to any one of them, and often reduces satisfaction with whatever gets chosen. The insight: Johnson's single-throw tactic isn't primarily a courage move, it's a cognitive-load move. Eliminating alternatives doesn't just prevent retreat — it frees the mental capacity previously spent maintaining and evaluating those alternatives, which is a real, measurable resource returned directly to the one thing left.

## The Live Edge

### Sharpest Implication

The most useful of the three is the one nobody runs. Johnson and Caesar both acted under visible pressure that made the choice legible, even urgent. Crawford acted with nothing wrong at all — and that's the version most people need and almost never take, because comfort produces no signal, and by the time it does the decline has usually already happened.

### Generative Questions

- Which of the three actually matches your current situation — and are you reaching for a different one because it's more dramatic or more familiar?
- Johnson's win made him a legend; the identical campaign, lost, would have made him a cautionary tale. What are you currently attributing to strategy that might mostly be outcome?
- Crawford left when nothing was wrong. What in your own life is currently fine, comfortable, and quietly no longer difficult?

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/strategy-4-the-death-ground-strategy|Strategy 4: The Death-Ground Strategy]] — the mechanism these three tactics operationalize
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/cortes-and-the-burnt-ships|Cortés and the Burnt Ships]] — the coercive version of the same principle
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/dostoyevskys-mock-execution|Dostoyevsky's Mock Execution]] — the involuntary version, and the maintenance problem it exposes

# Unverified Dogma Collects Dust

## Nobody Bothered

The explanation offered for accumulated strangeness is a null one, and its being null is the point.

> "**This is one of the reasons we have so many strange dogmas passed down within cultures and religions; no one has bothered to verify them to correct them.**"[^1]

**No one has bothered.** Not suppression, not deception, not a decision to preserve error. **An absence of action, sustained across generations.**

Which is a considerably better explanation than the conspiratorial one for most of what accumulates in any tradition. **Verification is work.** It takes time, it requires someone competent to do it, and — this is the operative part — **nobody's position depends on it being done.**

**And the default is retention.** A practice that is neither tested nor challenged simply continues, because continuing requires nothing. **Removal requires a decision; persistence does not.**

**Which makes accumulation the expected state of any long-running tradition**, and it does not need anyone to be at fault. A body of material that has run for a thousand years, with no one whose job is to check it, **will contain a thousand years of unchecked material.**

The image that names the state: "**the dust collects on everything after a while.**"[^1] **Dust settles on whatever is not being handled.** It does not indicate that anything went wrong; it indicates that nothing has been touched. See [[ARCHIVES/concepts/cross-domain/masters-test-the-old-texts-on-themselves|Masters Test the Old Texts on Themselves]].

## Even When Corrected

The second half is the harder finding, and it is about what happens when the work *is* done.

> "**Even when corrected, many will still cling to the past because ignorant people are often afraid to kill off ancient traditions even when they are harmful or wrong.**"[^1]

**Correction is not the binding constraint.** Which is the observation that makes this more than a complaint about laziness — **the material can be verified, found wrong, and retained anyway.**

**And the named motive is fear rather than stubbornness**: *afraid to kill off ancient traditions.*

**Which is a real and defensible fear**, and the passage's dismissal of it as ignorance is the weakest thing here. **A tradition is a system whose parts are not separable by inspection.** Removing an element that appears useless can remove something load-bearing that nobody had identified — **and a person unwilling to prune a thousand-year-old practice on one generation's assessment is exercising a reasonable caution.**

**The counter-argument is available in the same material and is not made**: the practices in question are *harmful, incorrect, ignorant, or just outdated*, and a tradition retaining harmful practices out of reverence has already stopped being a repository of anything.

**Both positions are real**, and this page states one and calls the other ignorance. 🚩 CONSENSUS MISREPRESENTATION.

**What survives regardless is the structural point.** **Verification and adoption are separate problems.** Solving the first does nothing about the second, and a tradition can be simultaneously well-audited and unchanged. See [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/be-a-lion-not-a-sheep|Be a Lion, Not a Sheep]].

## Four Ways a Practice Can Be Wrong

The final clause supplies a taxonomy, and the categories are not equivalent.

> Practices that should have been abandoned ages ago are maintained "**even though harmful, incorrect, ignorant, or just outdated.**"[^1]

**Four failure modes, and they call for different responses.**

**Harmful** — the practice does damage. **The only category with any urgency**, and the only one where retention has a victim.

**Incorrect** — the practice is based on a claim that is false. It may still work; a great many effective techniques rest on wrong explanations.

**Ignorant** — the practice reflects a state of knowledge that has been superseded. **Which is not the same as incorrect**: an ignorant practice may be right by accident.

**And just outdated** — fitted to conditions that no longer obtain. **The most common by far**, and the least culpable. A dietary rule for a climate, a schedule for an agricultural year, a prohibition answering a hazard that has gone.

**The word *just* is doing real work in that fourth item.** It concedes that the outdated practice was correct when adopted — **which means the tradition did its job and the world moved.**

Which sharpens what the audit should actually look for. **Harmful first, and the rest at leisure**, because only the first category has a cost that accrues while you deliberate.

**And it identifies why the audit rarely happens.** Three of the four categories describe practices that are doing no damage. **Nobody is motivated to remove something merely obsolete**, and by the time enough obsolete material has accumulated to matter, nobody can tell which is which. See [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/rules-as-the-path-is-the-lowest-rung|Rules as the Path Is the Lowest Rung]].

## Analytical Case Study: An Absence Presented as a Cause

The argument's logical shape is worth examining because it is unusual and slightly slippery.

**The claim is that unverified dogma persists *because* nobody verified it.**

**Which is not a cause.** It is the absence of a corrective, presented as an explanation for the thing the corrective would have removed.

**Compare two candidate explanations for the same observation.**

**A tradition retains strange material because forces preserve it** — institutional interest, doctrinal commitment, deliberate transmission. **This is a causal claim with predictions**: you could look for the forces, find who benefits, and check whether removing them changes anything.

**A tradition retains strange material because nothing removes it.** Which predicts nothing except that the material will still be there — **and that is what was observed.**

**The null explanation is nonetheless the better one**, and the reason is that retention is the default state. **Persistence needs no cause.** What needs explaining is not why unverified material stayed, but **why anyone imagined it would leave.**

**Which is where the argument earns its place.** The intuition it corrects is that traditions self-correct — that error gets noticed, that bad practices die out, that time is a filter. **It says time is not a filter and there is no mechanism**, and it names the one thing that could serve as one: masters testing the old texts on themselves.

**And the case study's finding is that this is a very weak corrective.** It happens rarely, mostly to people without teachers, one claim at a time, at a few weeks per claim, **and its results do not propagate** — because the second half of this page says corrections are not adopted anyway.

`[n=0 CASES]` — no dogma is named, no correction described, and no tradition examined.

## Implementation Workflow

**The audit is available to anyone and the sorting matters more than the verdict.**

**Start with the harmful category and stop there if you have limited time.** Three of the four failure modes cost nothing while you deliberate. **One of them has a victim.**

**For anything else, ask which of the four it is.** A practice that is merely outdated was correct once and its retention is inertia rather than error — **which changes both the urgency and the tone of the conversation.**

**Expect verification and adoption to be separate battles.** Establishing that something is wrong is the easier half, and this page's finding is that it accomplishes very little on its own. **Plan for the second problem before spending on the first.**

**And take the preservationist's objection seriously rather than calling it ignorance.** *Afraid to kill off ancient traditions* names a real risk: **a practice whose function nobody has identified may still have one.** The reasonable version of the audit removes the harmful and marks the rest rather than pruning it.

**Apply it to your own practice first.** The mechanism is general and does not exempt anyone — **whatever you are doing that you have never tested is collecting dust by the same process**, and you are not more likely to notice it than anybody else was.

**What this does not license:** discarding on the strength of one assessment. The material's own account of verification is that it is slow, single-subject, and produces results that may not generalise. See [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-dakini-who-invented-a-method|The Dakini Who Invented a Method]].

## Why It Falls to Masters Without Teachers

The one corrective named has a very specific demographic, and the demographic explains its weakness.

> "**Spiritual masters — and most often those without teachers themselves — often test cultivation practices that have been written about in ancient texts to verify them like this.**"[^2]

**Most often those without teachers.**

**Which means the verification happens where the transmission has already failed.** A practitioner with a living teacher asks; **one without a teacher has only the texts and their own body**, and testing is what remains.

**Three consequences, and they are all limiting.**

**The auditors are rare.** People with enough attainment to run the tests and no teacher to ask is a small population by construction.

**Their findings do not enter a lineage.** Someone outside a transmission chain has nowhere to put a correction — **which is precisely the adoption problem stated from the other end.**

**And the audit is driven by need rather than by coverage.** They test what they happen to be practising, not what most needs checking.

**Which produces a strange situation.** The tradition's checking is done by the people least connected to it, at their own pace, on their own selection, with no channel for the results.

**And it explains the dust.** Not that nobody ever verifies anything — **that verification and transmission run in different places and rarely meet.** See [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/the-east-outperforms-the-west-structurally|The East Outperforms the West Structurally]].

## Practices That Should Have Been Abandoned Ages Ago

The verdict is stated at maximum scope and it is worth noting what would be required to support it.

> Such practices "**are maintained in societies even though harmful, incorrect, ignorant, or just outdated.**"[^1]

**Maintained in societies** — the claim is about cultures and religions generally, not about any one.

**And nothing is named.** No practice, no tradition, no period, no case where a verification was performed and the result rejected.

**Which leaves the argument in a familiar condition**: a mechanism that is plausible and general, asserted about everyone, with the one thing that would test it absent.

**The mechanism is worth keeping regardless, because it is checkable in principle by anyone.** Take any tradition, including your own; **find a practice; ask when anyone last established that it does what it claims.** The prediction is that for most practices the answer is *nobody knows*, and that is a prediction a person can test in an afternoon.

**And the prediction is not obviously wrong.** Very little of what any culture does has ever been assessed against its stated purpose — **not because assessment is forbidden but because nothing occasions it.**

**What the page overreaches on is the verdict rather than the mechanism.** *Should have been abandoned ages ago* presumes the audit was run and the results are known. **The whole argument is that it was not run.** See [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/all-religions-will-disappear|All Religions Will Disappear]].

## What Verification Would Have to Establish

The audit sounds straightforward and it is not, because most inherited practices do not come with the thing a test needs.

**A test requires a stated claim.** *This produces that, in this timeframe.* **Verification is the comparison of an outcome against a prediction**, and where there is no prediction there is nothing to compare.

**And most transmitted practice has no stated claim at all.**

**Some have one and it is checkable.** *Concentrate here and the chi will clear in that region.* **A practitioner can run it.**

**Some have one and it is not.** *This accumulates merit for a future life.* **The claim is clear and the test is unavailable to anyone living.**

**And most have none.** A prohibition with no stated rationale, a form performed because it is performed, a sequence whose reason nobody recorded. **These cannot fail a test**, because there is nothing they were claimed to do.

**Which is where the four categories bite differently.** *Harmful* can be assessed without any stated claim — **damage is observable regardless of what anyone intended.** *Incorrect* needs a claim to be incorrect about. *Outdated* needs a purpose that conditions have moved away from.

**So the audit that is actually runnable is narrower than the one proposed**: **look for harm, which needs no stated purpose, and test claims where claims exist.** The residue — practices with no claim and no visible harm — **cannot be verified and cannot be shown to be dust either.**

Which is the honest limit, and it explains the accumulation better than *nobody bothered* does. **A great deal of what any tradition carries is untestable in principle**, and untestable material is not retained through negligence. **There was never a procedure that would have removed it.** See [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/be-a-lion-not-a-sheep|Be a Lion, Not a Sheep]].

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

**Evidence.** `[PRACTITIONER SOURCE]`. 🚩 SINGLE SOURCE. 🚩 CONSENSUS MISREPRESENTATION — *ignorant people* characterises everyone who preserves a tradition, and *so many strange dogmas passed down within cultures and religions* is an aggregate with nothing named. `[SPECULATIVE]`.

**Tension — nobody verifies, and the verdict presumes verification.** The argument is that these practices were never tested. The conclusion is that they *should have been abandoned ages ago*, which requires knowing they fail.

**Tension — preservation as ignorance, and the material's own caution about pruning.** The fear of killing off a tradition is called ignorance here. Elsewhere this material treats the loss of traditional technique as the central catastrophe of religious history — **which is the preservationist's position exactly.**

**Tension — a corrective run by outsiders.** The named verifiers are masters without teachers, whose results have no route back into a lineage. **The one repair mechanism is structurally disconnected from the thing it repairs.**

**Open question — what does a correction look like when it succeeds?** No case is described in which a practice was tested, found wanting, and dropped by anyone.

**Open question — how would a practice's function be established?** The four failure modes presume that a practice's purpose is knowable. Much of what any tradition does has no stated purpose to test against.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Two positions on inherited material run through this material and this page holds the corrosive one.

**Prune it.** Nobody verifies; the dust collects; practices that should have been abandoned are maintained; countless cherished dogmas would fail a scoring system; abandon what is false and replace what should be replaced.

**And it is nearly all we have.** The high teachings are being lost; the West already lost its explanations; no one can promise correct teachings will be available in future lives; support and re-establish genuine cultivation teachings; use the proven visualisations that have worked for countless people.

**These do not sit together comfortably**, and the tension is sharpest in the preservationist's fear that this page dismisses. **Someone afraid to kill off an ancient tradition is expressing the same concern the rest of this material expresses at length** — that these things are perishable, that the loss is usually permanent, and that nobody notices until it is gone.

**The convergence is on what would settle it, and it is the same in both directions: attainment present.** A tradition with someone who has reached the state can prune safely, because the pruner can tell what is load-bearing. **Without one, both the pruning and the preserving are guesses** — and the whole disagreement is between two ways of guessing.

Which locates the real claim. **This is not an argument for scepticism over reverence.** It is an argument that a tradition without living attainment has no way to maintain itself in either direction, and will accumulate dust whether it prunes or not. See [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/lao-tzu-never-described-a-chakra|Lao Tzu Never Described a Chakra]] and [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/zhu-xi-and-aquinas|Zhu Xi and Aquinas]].

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

**[[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/single-piece-feedback-rule-trainability-inversely-correlated|The Single-Piece Feedback Rule]]** — business.

The audit problem here is treated as one of *whether* correction happens. The training literature says the harder variable is *how fast*, and it supplies the mechanism that explains why traditions cannot self-correct at all.

The rule: **one piece of feedback at a time.** The common failure is a manager who watches a recording, sees twelve things to fix, and names all twelve — **and the person cannot act on twelve.** They freeze, pick one at random, or become demoralised. **The training looked like coaching and produced no behaviour change.**

And the law underneath: **trainability is inversely correlated with feedback latency.** The faster the feedback after the behaviour, the fewer repetitions needed to install the correction — **observed across species and skill domains**, not a management heuristic.

Three things fall out.

**A tradition's feedback latency is measured in centuries.** A practice is performed; whether it works is discovered — if ever — generations later, by someone else, who cannot tell the original practitioner. **At that latency the correlation says trainability is approximately zero.** Which is a stronger claim than *nobody bothered*: **even a tradition that did bother could not learn**, because the loop is too long to close.

**And it explains the four-category taxonomy's uselessness in practice.** Twelve things at once is the failure mode; **a tradition presented with an audit of everything it does is the same failure at scale.** The corrections cannot be absorbed, and the response is the one the sales case predicts — freeze, or pick one arbitrarily, or reject the whole assessment.

**Which reframes the preservationist as reasonable rather than ignorant.** Refusing a wholesale correction is what an organism does when handed twelve pieces of feedback. **The fix is not to insist harder; it is to deliver one.**

The insight neither field produces alone: **verification is not the bottleneck and adoption is not stubbornness.** Both are consequences of latency — a tradition receives its feedback too late and too much at once for any correction to install. **Which is why the one corrective this page names is a solo practitioner running a single test over a few weeks**: short latency, one piece of feedback, one subject. **The only working audit is the one nobody can scale**, and its non-scalability is the same property that makes it work.

## The Live Edge

The unresolved thing is **whether the corrections that were made are visible at all.**

The page's picture is of a tradition where nothing gets checked and dust accumulates uniformly. **And a tradition that had corrected itself would look identical.**

**Consider what a successful correction leaves behind.** A practice was tested, found wanting, and dropped. **The dropped practice is not in the tradition.** The correction is not recorded, because nobody documents the absence of something. **What remains is the surviving material, which looks exactly like material that was never examined.**

**Which means the evidence for *nobody bothered* is the presence of strange practices** — and the presence of strange practices is compatible with any amount of prior pruning, since pruning removes and does not annotate.

**Three readings, and nothing here chooses.**

**Nothing was ever checked**, and everything strange is unexamined residue. **Which is the page's claim and is the strongest version.**

**A great deal was checked and dropped**, and what survives is the residue that passed — in which case the strangeness of the survivors is evidence about how strange the discarded material was, and the tradition has been working.

**Or checking happened unevenly** — heavily in some areas, never in others — which would make a blanket verdict useless and a targeted audit essential.

**The stake is what a practitioner should assume about an inherited practice they cannot evaluate.** Under the first reading, assume nothing has been tested and treat everything as unverified. **Under the second, assume survival is weak evidence of having passed something** — which is the track-record argument this material makes elsewhere about the proven visualisations.

**And that is the direct contradiction.** *Use the practices that have worked for countless people* treats survival as evidence. **This page treats survival as evidence of nothing but inertia.** Both are stated, and they cannot both be the general rule.

# The Results Fallacy and the Income Lock

## If It Doesn't Work, Why Is It Working?

Somebody starts doing something, and things start happening that weren't happening before.

Here's the inference they draw, given in their own voice:

> If something produces results where there were none previously, then of course people will think this is progress even if it's the incorrect way. **If it wasn't the right way to cultivate, they reason, how could it produce psychic abilities?**[^1]

That isn't a stupid argument. It's a perfectly ordinary appeal to evidence — the method has an output, the output is real, so the method does something. Everything up to that point holds.

## Real Method, Real Output, Real Danger

The failure is in the last step, and almost nobody notices themselves taking it: from *this method produces effects* to *this method produces the effect I want.* Two different claims. The results establish the first. They don't touch the second.

The case here is an unusually clean demonstration, because the method produces genuine, impressive output *and* is held to be actively dangerous. The practitioners are cultivating the *du-yin* — the image-faculty that runs without any sensory input, the shadowed half of the ordinary sorting mind — and it works. When various small superpowers appear out of the obstruction and the unclarity it produces, **most people actually think this is something special.**[^1]

The verdict on the method producing them: *cultivating the du-yin is a dangerous activity because it is putting yourself on the very borders of insanity and is a state that never can be made clear.*[^1] Real method, real output, real danger — and the output is what convinces the practitioner to carry on.

The structure generalises a long way past this material. Any method producing any noticeable effect gets defended by that effect, whether the effect is the goal, a side product, or a symptom. And the more striking the effect, the harder the defence — so **the methods most likely to entrench are the ones with the most dramatic by-products**, not the ones that work best.

## Right on Small Things, Wrong on Big Ones

The output has a shape, and the shape is where the argument actually gets settled. Not how much of it there is — what kind.

Because it's free of the confines of the senses, the solitary consciousness can sometimes operate outside the normal limits of space and time, which is why people sometimes know things about the future.[^2] Then the qualifier:

> You can know small things because the du-yin has been operating free of space and time, but of course this potential only exists in regards to small things. **It's never accurate in regards to big matters, which is why some psychics are right on small issues and wrong on the big picture.**[^2]

That's a signature rather than a score, and it's what makes the evidence readable. A method whose hit rate is real, frequent, and confined to things that were never going to change a decision is producing exactly what you'd expect from something that isn't reaching outside you at all.

And the whole class of output carries a stamp: the du-yin is the shadow or unclear side of the sorting mind, so even when it produces psychic phenomena, **they will still be unclear**.[^2] The unclarity isn't a defect of a particular practitioner. It's a property of the faculty.

## Nobody Chose This

The part that changes the moral shape of the whole thing is how people arrive in the state. It isn't by picking a bad method.

> many people who meditate fall into the shadow functioning of the du-yin simply because **their chi can't initially penetrate through the hind region of the brain**, and through improper instructions they latch onto this somewhat confused mental state of unclarity and begin to feel that it is the correct way to cultivate.[^1]

Two things had to go wrong together. A blockage, which is physical and nobody's fault — the energy meets a hard place at the back of the head and doesn't get through. And then bad instruction, which tells the practitioner that what they've landed in is where they were going.

So the person defending the method isn't defending a choice. They're defending a place they ended up in, described to them by somebody they trusted, and confirmed weekly by results that are perfectly real.

The same trap catches serious people at much higher levels. A practitioner called Chin reached a realm where nothing moved at all, and stayed in it for more than half a month:

> Unfortunately, I had not met a venerable adept with an enlightened eye and the skillful technique to break up this realm for me. **I should not have settled down here.** Of this it is said, "If you do not get free of your perception of truth, it blocks correct perception."[^3]

*Your perception of truth blocks correct perception.* Not your error. The thing you actually saw, correctly, is what's now in the way — and what would have got him out wasn't a better argument. It was somebody who could recognise the realm and break it up for him, and there wasn't one.

## The Second Lock

Then, in the same sentence as the results fallacy, a second thing gets named that holds these practitioners in place, and it has nothing to do with what they believe:

> It's often impossible to convince these people that their cultivation methodology is all wrong, especially when **they're getting results or making their living out of it.**[^1]

*Or making their living out of it.* Two locks in one clause, and they're different mechanisms that happen to hold the same door.

**The first lock is about believing.** The person has evidence, has drawn a conclusion, and the conclusion is wrong in a subtle way. In principle a better argument or a better piece of evidence could reach them — that's what the analysis of the faculty is for.

**The second is about paying.** It doesn't work on what somebody believes; it works on what it would **cost** them to revise. Anyone who teaches, charges, or has built a reputation and a livelihood on a method isn't weighing the argument on its merits, because the merits stopped being the only thing in the balance.

And *impossible* is the right word. Not difficult. And the impossibility doesn't imply bad faith — which is what makes the second lock so much worse than the first, since there's nobody to persuade and nothing dishonest to expose.

The sharpest statement of the cost is a line from much later in the same book: **to cheat others as a way of making a living is one thing, but to cut off your wisdom life by cheating yourself is another.**[^4] The income lock is usually discussed as a problem for the audience. It's stated here as a problem for the person holding it.

## Why Small Results Lock Harder Than Big Ones

There's a feature of the results lock the passage implies without stating, and it inverts what you'd expect. The practitioners in view are producing **small** superpowers — minor, unclear, arriving out of what's described as an unclear stupor.[^1] Not levitation. Small things: knowing something, sensing something, being right about a detail.

Those lock hardest, and for three reasons that all point the same way. None of them has anything to do with the results being good.

**They're frequent.** A large result happens once and becomes a story. A small result happens weekly and becomes a *pattern* — and to the person having it, a pattern is far better evidence than one spectacular event.

**They're unfalsifiable at exactly the right size.** A claim to fly is checkable and fails in public. A claim to have sensed something is never quite wrong, because the hits are real and the misses were never written down.

**And they're cheap enough to keep coming.** A method that occasionally delivers something enormous has long droughts in which doubt can get in. A method delivering something modest every week never leaves the gap.

So lock strength isn't proportional to how impressive the output is. **It's proportional to the output's frequency and its resistance to being checked** — which is exactly the class of result this passage is about, and a great deal of what any method in any field delivers to the people running it. The uncomfortable version for the commercial case: steady modest returns nobody can attribute cleanly are harder to walk away from than occasional spectacular ones. **The unremarkable results are the sticky ones.**

## Analytical Case Study: The Madman Who Is Sometimes Right

The cleanest demolition of the results fallacy in this material is one sentence about somebody nobody would take advice from.

> Even an insane or crazy person, who is operating within the du-yin most of the time, **can sometimes make remarkably accurate and thus unnerving comments** due to the workings of the solitary consciousness, but that doesn't mean that the individual is cultivating, nor that they're sane in the first place. It doesn't make their prognostications trustworthy either.[^2]

Picture the man on the ward who says something about your father that he had no way of knowing, and is right. Everybody in the room feels it. And nobody concludes that his condition is a spiritual method or that he should be consulted about anything else.

That's the whole argument, and it works because the conclusion is already obvious in his case. He produces genuine, striking, unnerving output. He is on the same faculty as the practitioner — more of the time, in fact. And the output tells you nothing whatever about whether he's going anywhere, because he isn't going anywhere.

So the inference *it produced a result, therefore the method is right* has a counterexample that requires no doctrine to accept. Anybody would refuse the inference about the madman. The only question is why they accept it about themselves, and the answer is the second half of the sentence — he isn't cultivating and isn't sane, and you are, so the identical output must mean something different in your case.

It doesn't. Same faculty, same unclarity, same restriction to small things. What's different is the story attached to it.

## Implementation Workflow

This diagnostic runs on anybody in any field, and the two locks need testing separately, because a fix for one does nothing for the other. **For the results lock, write down what the method was supposed to do — before you look at what it produced.** Then compare. The failure isn't that nothing happened. It's that something happened and the goal quietly moved to match it. If your original statement of purpose no longer sounds like what you'd say now, the method has renegotiated the target and you weren't at the meeting.

Then check the **shape** of the results rather than their volume. Are they frequent, modest, and hard to attribute cleanly? That's the sticky profile, and it's the one that survives longest without being right. Are you recording the misses anywhere? If not, the hit rate you believe in is a number nobody has ever computed.

**For the income lock, the test is a price rather than an argument.** Ask what it would cost you to conclude the method was wrong — in money, in reputation, in what you'd have to tell people who took your advice. Write the figure down. You're not deciding anything with it. You're establishing that the figure exists, because the whole mechanism runs on it being invisible.

And if the number is large, stop trying to reason yourself out of it. Nobody in that position weighs an argument on its merits, and knowing that about yourself is worth more than another round of thinking about it. What works instead is structural: get the judgement made by somebody who isn't paid either way, or set the criterion in advance, while the cost of being wrong is still hypothetical.

**The one thing that would have saved Chin was a person, not an idea.**[^3] Somebody with the eye to recognise the realm he'd settled into and the technique to break it up. If your field has such people, the useful question is whether you know one — and if it doesn't, that's worth knowing too.

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

Ranges read: pp. 444 and 594, with footnote 518 at p. 511 checked in place. Nothing here is claimed about material outside them. `[POPULAR SOURCE]`. Chin's motionless realm reaches this vault at second hand, quoted from Nan Huai-Chin's *To Realize Enlightenment* in J. C. Cleary's translation.[^3]

🚩 **Shamans are named as the perfect example** of people who cultivate the du-yin and who therefore *can offer very little in terms of true knowledge*, having chosen a state of uncontrolled imagery and unclear stupor.[^1] That's a characterisation of many living traditions, offered with no case, no source, and no distinction drawn between them. Recorded as the source's position, not adopted, and nothing on this page rests on it.

🚩 The cold-water passage lists what people who believe themselves enlightened cannot do — control their dreams, be aware while asleep, demonstrate any samādhi, produce a transformation body, communicate with spiritual beings — ending with *and their legs still hurt when they meditate!*[^4] And then, immediately: *these aren't, of course, any proof of enlightenment in the first place.* The list is admitted to be a list of non-proofs and is deployed as a rebuke anyway. The tension the material leaves standing is that both locks get diagnosed and only one gets a remedy. The results lock has an answer — understand the faculty, learn its signature, watch the shape of your own output. The income lock is called *impossible* and then nothing follows.[^1] The person most in need of the argument is the person the argument says it cannot reach, and no structural alternative is offered.

A second tension is that the same signature gets two different mechanisms in this corpus. Small things right and big things absent is explained here by the solitary consciousness operating free of space and time,[^2] and elsewhere by an assembly of stored experience. Both are printed, both predict the identical profile, and nothing distinguishes them.

**Open questions.** If the income lock really is impossible to argue past, what has ever actually changed anybody's method in a field where their livelihood depended on it — and was it ever an argument? And has anybody kept the misses? The whole results lock rests on a hit rate nobody has computed.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Two ways of holding the results fallacy, and they lead to different behaviour toward other people. Take it as an error of reasoning and the response is instruction. The person made a bad inference, so you show them the inference — two claims, only one established, and here's the madman as a counterexample. That treats them as mistaken and correctable, and it's what the analysis of the faculty is written for.

Take it as a position rather than a belief and instruction is beside the point. Somebody whose livelihood rests on the method isn't reasoning about it, and telling them so changes nothing except how they feel about you. That treats them as located rather than mistaken, and it points at structure — criteria set in advance, judgement made by somebody with no stake — instead of at argument.

Both appear in a single sentence, and the second quietly undercuts the first.[^1] The cold-water list is the same problem in action: a rebuke aimed at people the surrounding argument says can't be reached, made of items the passage concedes prove nothing.[^4]

Read against [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/du-yin-and-the-psi-programmes|Du-Yin and the Psi Programmes]], the faculty is that page's territory and this one carries what believing its output costs. Against [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/superpowers-are-not-evidence|Superpowers Are Not Evidence]], this is the same doctrine stated as a business problem rather than a doctrinal one. And [[ARCHIVES/concepts/cross-domain/cameron-and-the-self-deception-of-the-researcher|Cameron and the Self-Deception of the Researcher]] is the income lock operating on somebody with a laboratory instead of a clientele.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

Behavioral mechanics — [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/grace-and-chosenness-as-institutional-excuses|Grace and Chosenness as Institutional Excuses]]. That page's mechanism is a doctrine explaining every failure as the petitioner's shortfall — exactly the kind of claim an institution would want, because it never returns a verdict against the institution.

The results fallacy is that structure running on an individual rather than an organisation, and setting them side by side shows what they share: **an interpretive rule that can only ever come out one way.** Under grace, a failure means you fell short and a success means the doctrine works. Under the results fallacy, an output is the method working and an absence is you not having practised enough. Nothing either believer could observe would count against what they hold.

What falls out of the pair is a test that doesn't require settling any of the substance. **Ask what result would count as evidence against, and check whether the answer is available before the fact.** Somebody who can't name one isn't holding a belief about the world. They're holding a position — and positions change by cost rather than by evidence.

It also explains why the income lock is the harder of the two. The cognitive version can in principle be broken by supplying the missing counterexample, which is what the madman does. The commercial and institutional versions can't, because the rule's one-sidedness is doing a job for somebody. A rule that pays its holder isn't a mistake. It's an arrangement.

*One handshake.* A second, on competitive pressure eventually forcing what argument can't, is carried by [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/religious-change-driven-by-competition-not-compassion|Religious Change Driven by Competition, Not Compassion]] and the pointer does the work.

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication.** The two locks want opposite responses and the same person usually has both. Argument works on the first and is wasted on the second, and there's no way to tell from outside which one you're addressing — so the reliable move is to stop arguing and change what the answer costs, which is the only lever that touches both.

**Generative questions.**
- Write down what your main method was supposed to do, from memory, before you check. Then check. Did the target move?
- What would it cost you — in money, in reputation, in conversations you'd have to have — to conclude that the thing you're best known for doesn't work? Write the figure down. Don't decide anything with it.
- Are you recording the misses? If not, the hit rate you're defending has never been computed by anybody, including you.

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/du-yin-and-the-psi-programmes|Du-Yin and the Psi Programmes]] — the faculty producing the results this page is about

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/false-stages-and-the-footnote-that-says-so|False Stages, and the Footnote That Says So]] — the ladder these results are being read against

# Adaptation as 60 Percent Original

## Bad Books Make Good Movies

Roth has spent sixty years adapting other people's material. Forrest Gump (novel). Benjamin Button (short story). Munich (history). Killers of the Flower Moon (nonfiction). He has a saying about it: *bad books make good movies. That's that's the slogan. Or bad plays make better movies.*[^1]

The throwaway line carries a real craft principle. Adaptation is not translation. A *good* book usually does its work too completely on the page to leave the screenwriter room to add. A *bad* book — meaning a book with a strong premise but uneven execution — leaves gaps the screenwriter fills. Roth's adaptations end up *60 to 70% original* despite being labeled adaptations.[^2] The premise stays. The structure shifts. The dialogue is mostly invented. The characters are deepened or restructured. The film becomes something the source seeded but didn't determine.

## What This Actually Is

Adaptation-as-60-percent-original is the *honest accounting* of what screenwriting adaptation actually is. The screenwriter is sometimes called a translator. They are usually a co-author of a different work that shares premise and characters with the source. The novel's interior consciousness becomes scenes. The novel's pacing becomes structure. The novel's themes become the spine. The novel's specific scenes are mostly invented anew.

## What Triggers the Need

Faithful adaptation usually fails. The Forrest Gump novel's Forrest *weighs 400 pounds*[^3] — Roth cut that, made him slim, changed the tone of the character. *Being an idiot is no box of chocolates* becomes *life is like a box of chocolates*. Roth made the changes because faithful translation would have produced a worse film. The principle isn't betrayal; it's adaptation-as-craft.

## The Mechanism

Three things drive the 60% original portion:

**Form difference.** Novel interior monologue can't be filmed. Scenes have to be invented to externalize what the novel told internally.

**Pacing difference.** Novels can spend chapters on what films can spend two minutes on. Whole subplots get compressed, transposed, or invented.

**Audience difference.** Novel readers commit to a sustained experience. Film viewers commit to two hours. Material that works for one fails for the other and has to be reshaped.

## Synergies & Handshakes

Adaptation-as-60-percent-original gives Roth's other craft principles room to operate. Theme-as-rudder can dominate adaptations because the source's theme can be made more explicit. Find-a-home opening can be redesigned for film. Dialogue economy can replace novel exposition. The 60% original is where the screenwriter's craft lives.

## Analytical Case Study: Forrest Gump Adaptation Choices

The novel's Forrest weighs 400 pounds, is more savvy, and the tone is more satirical. Roth's adaptation makes Forrest slim, slow, sincere. The change inverts the novel's affective register. The result is a film that's more emotionally available than the novel — a different work entirely while preserving the premise (a simple man traverses 20th-century American history).

Roth also added the bench framing. The novel doesn't have Forrest sitting at a bus stop telling his life story to strangers. Roth invented the framing because the film needed a structural device the novel didn't provide. Pure invention. Foundational to what the film became.

## Implementation Workflow

You're adapting source material. Read the source three times. Make a list. Column one: what's load-bearing about this material that must stay. Column two: what works on the page but won't work on screen. Column three: what's missing that the film will need to invent.

Now write the screenplay from column one and column three. Column two is the source's success that you're discarding. Don't apologize for the discarding. The film is a different work.

## The Failure (Diagnostic Signs)

You'll know adaptation has gone wrong when the resulting script reads as *the book with parts cut out*. The cut version is shorter but not better. The discipline is to *replace* what's cut with film-native invention. Subtraction without invention produces thin adaptations.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

MacCulloch's discipline of fidelity-to-historical-record sits opposite Roth's 60% original. The historian who took Roth's adaptation approach would be a fictionalizer. The screenwriter who took MacCulloch's approach would produce stage-readings, not films. Different forms, different fidelity requirements.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

- **Creative-practice**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/bilton-narrative-nonfiction-methodology|Bilton Narrative Nonfiction Methodology]] — the narrative-nonfiction parallel of constrained-but-original work. Bilton's true-events-with-narrative-craft is structurally analogous to Roth's source-with-invention. Both writers operate inside fidelity constraints while doing the inventive work the form requires.
- **History**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/historical-fiction-as-research-driven-imagination|Historical Fiction as Research-Driven Imagination]] — historical-fiction craft sits between strict history and free invention. Roth's adaptation principle operates at the same boundary in a different register. Both forms invent within constraint; the constraint differs.

The compound insight: adaptation, narrative nonfiction, and historical fiction are all *constrained-invention* forms. The constraint is what gives the invention shape. Pure invention has no shape; pure faithfulness has no breath. The polymath read: most powerful writing operates in the constrained-invention zone, and the writer's craft is the calibration of how much constraint to honor against how much to invent.

## The Live Edge

**The Sharpest Implication**

If you're working on an adaptation and feeling guilty about how much you're changing, the diagnosis is that you've internalized a wrong model of what adaptation is. Adaptation is co-authorship. The 60% original is the work the form requires of you. The guilt is the symptom; the craft is the cure.

**Generative Questions**

- For a current adaptation, what percentage is original? If it's much below 60%, the form is probably suffering. If much above 80%, the source may not have been load-bearing.
- What's the equivalent of adaptation-as-60-percent-original in other forms? When you translate an essay into a talk, a book into an article, a research paper into a popular piece — does the same percentage hold?
